title: SYSK Selects: What Makes a One-hit Wonder?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on one-hit wonders, originally published March 2008 (the intro says "two thousand and" with the year cut off; the rerun date is January 2018). Josh and Chuck discuss the origin of the phrase (earliest print use cited as a July 1977 article about ABBA), the Billboard top forty definition and why it gets blurry, and examples across decades from the 1950s through the 2000s, including songs like Green Tambourine, Spirit in the Sky, Funky Town, Take On Me, Too Shy and Africa-style one-hit bands. They extend the idea beyond music to baseball (Eddie Gaedel's walk, Chris Jelic's home run), art (Harvey Ball's smiley face, Grant Wood's American Gothic), and books and film (To Kill a Mockingbird, The Catcher in the Rye, A Confederacy of Dunces, Heaven's Gate, Arthur). The episode closes with listener mail from a listener whose wife thinks the hosts are stoners.
topics: British music in the US and Europe

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the SYSK Selects rerun of the one-hit wonder episode, originally published in March 2008, and jokes about artists being annoyed at the term. Chuck and Josh open the conversation, mention a documentary idea about the psychology of being a one-hit wonder, and note there is little scholarly research on the topic.

segments.title: Origin of the phrase and the definition
segments.summary: The hosts say the origin of 'one hit wonder' is uncertain. Phrases.org cites a July 1977 print use about ABBA as the earliest known appearance in print. The generally held definition requires a Billboard Top 40 hit, which the hosts note becomes blurry in practice.

segments.title: One-hit wonders beyond the top forty
segments.summary: The hosts discuss artists with only one hit who are still legendary, such as Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin, and songs that were cultural hits without top forty chart placement, such as Wall of Voodoo's Mexican Radio. They note the term is often used as a derogatory label.

segments.title: One-hit wonders by decade in music
segments.summary: The hosts run through one-hit wonders across the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, including Green Tambourine, Spirit in the Sky, Seasons in the Sun, and Right Said Fred, and note that disco produced many one-hit acts because it was producer-driven. They also discuss bands popular abroad such as Aha, Falco and Nena.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in sports
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the term in baseball, noting players with a single hit, including Chris Jelic who hit a home run and Eddie Gaedel, who drew four walks in one plate appearance for the 1951 Yankees and whose jersey is in the Hall of Fame.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in art
segments.summary: Harvey Ball, who created the smiley face as a marketing campaign for State Mutual Life Assurance and was paid two dollars, is discussed as an art example. Grant Wood, painter of American Gothic, is also mentioned, and the hosts describe his struggles with fame and his reported withdrawal from painting.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in books and film
segments.summary: The hosts discuss authors with one famous novel, including Harper Lee (To Kill a Mockingbird), J.D. Salinger, John Kennedy Toole (A Confederacy of Dunces, published after his death), Sylvia Plath, and Joseph Heller. They then cover film figures such as Michael Cimino (The Deer Hunter, then Heaven's Gate), and Steve Gordon (Arthur), and the hosts' dislike of the Arthur remake.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener writes that his wife believes the hosts are stoners and asks for a shout-out to her. The hosts respond humorously and then close with the usual calls to action, including the show's website and social media.
